title: Stage 9, Lesson 4: Credit score - why it matters
subtitle: Your borrowing and repayment history sets what borrowing costs you in future
openingQuestion: Two people borrow 500 million for a car from the same bank. A has years of on-time repayments; B has been late on a credit card a few times. What usually differs between the two loans?
openingOptions: Nothing differs, because the amount borrowed is the same
B faces a higher rate or has to put up collateral
A always pays a higher rate for having borrowed several times before
Banks are not permitted to use credit history when setting a rate
explanation: A credit score, or credit history, is how lenders quantify the risk that someone defaults, based on how they have borrowed and repaid in the past. A good repayment record usually comes with a better rate and a higher limit; a record of late payments makes the lender price the extra risk in, through a higher rate or tighter conditions.

diagram.label: The national credit information centre (CIC) compiles it
A credit score or debt group
Sets the rate and the limit on future borrowing

realWorldExample.company: CIC - Vietnam's National Credit Information Centre
realWorldExample.description: CIC compiles individual borrowing and repayment history from lenders and sorts debt into groups from 1 (standard) to 5 (potential capital loss) - and one bad debt, however small, can affect your ability to borrow for a home or a car for years afterwards.

quiz.question: A small credit card balance (a few million dong) more than 90 days late - what can it do to a mortgage application five years later?
options: Yes - debt over 90 days is classified as bad debt
No - only debts above 100 million are recorded
Yes - but the effect only lasts three months
No - the amount is too small for the system to log
quiz.explanation: This is the single most important credit lesson: the size of the late balance does not set the size of the consequence. What decides it is the LENGTH of the delay and the classification into a bad-debt group, and that can follow you for years, into loans many times larger.

quiz.question: Why is "never borrow anything at all" not necessarily the best way to build a good credit history?
options: Because never borrowing puts you in the high-risk group
Because the system needs a borrowing record to assess you
Because banks prefer customers holding several loans
Because your score rises with the number of cards you hold
quiz.explanation: This is a common paradox: some credit assessment models run on a history of borrowing behaviour, so someone who has never borrowed and repaid anything also gives the system nothing to judge reliability by - even though they have no bad debt at all.

quiz.question: You cannot raise enough this month to clear the credit card balance. Which handling does least damage to your credit history?
options: Skip this month and pay two months together next time
Call the bank and ask to defer the whole payment cycle
Pay the minimum payment on time
Take cash from another card to make up the amount
quiz.explanation: The minimum payment still costs interest on the remaining balance, but it stops the clock on days overdue - a large difference over time. Taking cash from another card carries very high fees and interest, and only moves the problem somewhere more expensive.

quiz.question: After settling a bad debt, what happens to the credit history?
options: The debt is moved into a monitoring status
The record is erased the moment the debt is settled
The score returns immediately to its level before the debt
The record stays visible for a period of time
quiz.explanation: This is why one small late payment can affect a mortgage file years later. The consequence does not end at the moment you settle.

quiz.question: Why can using nearly the whole credit limit every month count against you even when you always pay in full and on time?
options: Because a high utilisation rate reads as a sign of dependence on credit
Because the bank charges interest on the limit used even when it is paid in full on time
Because every time you touch the ceiling it is recorded as a late repayment
Because the limit is cut automatically once a customer uses over half of it in a month
quiz.explanation: Repayment history and limit utilisation are two different signals. Constantly hitting the ceiling shows spending running close to capacity, which many institutions read as higher risk - even with a statement that has never carried a late payment.

keyTakeaways: Credit history reflects default risk and directly sets the rate and limit you are approved for in future
An overdue debt, however small, can still land in a bad-debt group and affect borrowing for years
CIC is where individual credit history is compiled in Vietnam

practicePrompt.question: You forget a credit card balance of only 500,000 dong for 3 months, assuming the amount is too small to matter. Two years later a bank turns down your mortgage application over bad credit history. What happened?
options: The bank refused for some other reason; a 500,000 dong debt is far too small to affect a later loan application
An overdue debt, however small, is still recorded by CIC and affects borrowing for years afterwards
Credit history is only retained for 3 months, so it cannot possibly affect a loan applied for 2 years later
Being refused a loan has nothing whatsoever to do with previous credit card repayment history
practicePrompt.explanation: An overdue debt, however small, can still land in a bad-debt group and affect borrowing for years. CIC compiles individual credit history in Vietnam, and it feeds directly into the rate and the limit you are approved for.

application.title: Check CIC before you need to borrow
application.message: Register on the CIC portal and read your own report now, not while a loan application is in progress. Errors - a closed card still showing a balance, a guarantee that is not yours - take time to dispute and correct.
application.secondary: One card left unpaid by 500 thousand for over 10 days still leaves a trace, and the trace travels with your mortgage file a few years later.

sections.text: A small credit card balance left late today can make a mortgage hard to get five years from now - which is why credit history matters more than most people assume.
Credit history sets what borrowing costs you later

A credit score or history is how lenders quantify default risk from past borrowing behaviour. Debt more than 90 days overdue is usually classified into a bad-debt group on the CIC system, and that record can be held for years - affecting far larger loans (a mortgage, for instance) later on, even where the original late amount was tiny.

sections.title: The five debt groups on the CIC system
sections.subtitle: Grouping is based mainly on the number of days overdue

concepts.def: Paid on time, or under 10 days late. This is the group to stay in if you plan to borrow a large sum later.
Roughly 10-90 days late. Not bad debt yet, but it is on record and can mean your loan file is examined more closely.
Roughly 91-180 days late. From this group onwards it counts as bad debt.
Roughly 181-360 days late. The chance of a new loan being approved is close to zero while it remains on record.
Over 360 days late. The effect runs for years, including after the debt has been settled.

sections.text: Four habits that keep a credit history clean

items: Set a reminder a few days before the card is due rather than relying on memory. Most jumps into a worse debt group come from forgetting, not from having no money.
Pay the minimum on time when the month is tight - the minimum still counts as on time, whereas paying nothing starts the clock on days overdue.
Be careful with small instalment loans from consumer finance companies: they are reported to CIC like any other borrowing.
Do not put your name to a loan for somebody else, or guarantee one, unless you are ready to repay it - on the system that is a debt in your name.

sections.label: Check your own record
sections.text: Individuals can look up their own credit information through CIC. Do it a few months before submitting a large loan application: if you find an error in what was recorded, you still have time to ask the lender to correct it, rather than being refused without understanding why.

One point people often misread: settling a bad debt does not erase the history immediately. The record is retained and visible for a set period after settlement, depending on the group. That means the consequence of a single late payment does not end at the moment you clear it - which is why prevention is far cheaper than repair here.

lines: Paying every loan on time, however small, is the cheapest investment you can make in your ability to borrow large later.
One late payment today can cost far more than the amount that was late.
